{{Short description|Theory in algebraic topology}}
[[File:Penrose-dreieck.svg|thumb|A [[Penrose triangle]] depicts a nontrivial element of the first cohomology of an [[annulus (mathematics)|annulus]] with values in the group of distances from the observer.<ref>{{Citation |first=Roger |last=Penrose |authorlink=Roger Penrose |date=1992 |title=On the Cohomology of Impossible Figures |journal=[[Leonardo (journal)|Leonardo]] |volume=25 |issue=3/4 |pages=245–247 |doi=10.2307/1575844|jstor=1575844 |s2cid=125905129 }}. Reprinted from {{Citation |first=Roger |last=Penrose |authorlink=Roger Penrose |date=1991 |title=On the Cohomology of Impossible Figures / La Cohomologie des Figures Impossibles |journal=Structural Topology |volume=17 |pages=11–16 |url=http://www.iri.upc.edu/people/ros/StructuralTopology/ST17/st17.html | accessdate = January 16, 2014}}</ref>]]

In [[mathematics]], specifically [[algebraic topology]], '''Čech cohomology''' is a [[cohomology]] theory based on the intersection properties of [[open set|open]] [[cover (topology)|covers]] of a [[topological space]]. It is named for the mathematician [[Eduard Čech]].

==Motivation==
Let ''X'' be a topological space, and let <math>\mathcal{U}</math> be an open cover of ''X''. Let <math>N(\mathcal{U})</math> denote the [[nerve of a covering|nerve]] of the covering. The idea of Čech cohomology is that, for an open cover <math>\mathcal{U}</math> consisting of sufficiently small open sets, the resulting [[Abstract simplicial complex|simplicial complex]] <math>N(\mathcal{U})</math> should be a good combinatorial model for the space ''X''. For such a cover, the Čech cohomology of ''X'' is defined to be the [[simplicial homology|simplicial]] [[cohomology]] of the nerve. This idea can be formalized by the notion of a [[good cover]]. However, a more general approach is to take the [[direct limit]] of the cohomology groups of the nerve over the system of all possible open covers of ''X'', ordered by [[Open cover#Refinement|refinement]]. This is the approach adopted below.

==Construction==

Let ''X'' be a [[topological space]], and let <math>\mathcal{F}</math> be a [[presheaf]] of [[abelian group]]s on ''X''. Let <math>\mathcal{U}</math> be an [[open cover]] of ''X''.

===Simplex===
A ''q''-'''simplex''' σ of <math>\mathcal{U}</math> is an ordered collection of ''q''+1 sets chosen from <math>\mathcal{U}</math>, such that the intersection of all these sets is non-empty. This intersection is called the ''support'' of σ and is denoted |σ|.

Now let <math>\sigma = (U_i)_{i \in \{ 0 , \ldots , q \}}</math> be such a ''q''-simplex. The ''j-th partial boundary'' of σ is defined to be the (''q''−1)-simplex obtained by removing the ''j''-th set from σ, that is: 

:<math>\partial_j \sigma := (U_i)_{i \in \{ 0 , \ldots , q \} \setminus \{j\}}.</math>

The ''boundary'' of σ is defined as the alternating sum of the partial boundaries:

:<math>\partial \sigma := \sum_{j=0}^q (-1)^{j+1} \partial_j \sigma</math>

viewed as an element of the [[free abelian group]] spanned by the simplices of <math>\mathcal{U}</math>.

===Cochain===
A ''q''-'''cochain''' of <math>\mathcal{U}</math> with coefficients in <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is a map which associates with each ''q''-simplex σ an element of <math>\mathcal{F}(|\sigma|)</math>, and we denote the set of all ''q''-cochains of <math>\mathcal{U}</math> with coefficients in <math>\mathcal{F}</math> by <math>C^q(\mathcal U, \mathcal F)</math>. <math>C^q(\mathcal U, \mathcal F)</math> is an abelian group by pointwise addition.

===Differential===
The cochain groups can be made into a [[cochain complex]] <math>(C^{\bullet}(\mathcal U, \mathcal F), \delta)</math> by defining the '''coboundary operator''' <math>\delta_q : C^q(\mathcal U, \mathcal F) \to C^{q+1}(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{F}) </math> by:

<math> \quad (\delta_q f)(\sigma) := \sum_{j=0}^{q+1} (-1)^j \mathrm{res}^{|\partial_j \sigma|}_{|\sigma|} f (\partial_j \sigma),</math>

where <math>\mathrm{res}^{|\partial_j \sigma|}_{|\sigma|}</math> is the [[Sheaf (mathematics)|restriction morphism]] from <math>\mathcal F(|\partial_j \sigma|)</math> to <math>\mathcal F(|\sigma|).</math> (Notice that ∂<sub>j</sub>σ ⊆ σ, but {{pipe}}σ{{pipe}} ⊆ {{pipe}}∂<sub>j</sub>σ{{pipe}}.)

A calculation shows that <math>\delta_{q+1} \circ \delta_q = 0.</math>

The coboundary operator is analogous to the [[exterior derivative]] of [[De Rham cohomology]], so it sometimes called 
the differential of the cochain complex.

====Cocycle====
A ''q''-cochain is called a ''q''-cocycle if it is in the kernel of <math>\delta</math>, hence <math>Z^q(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{F}) := \ker ( \delta_q) \subseteq C^q(\mathcal U, \mathcal F)</math> is the set of all ''q''-cocycles.

Thus a (''q''−1)-cochain <math>f</math> is a cocycle if for all ''q''-simplices <math>\sigma</math> the cocycle condition 

:<math>\sum_{j=0}^{q} (-1)^j \mathrm{res}^{|\partial_j \sigma|}_{|\sigma|} f (\partial_j \sigma) = 0</math> 

holds. 

A 0-cocycle <math>f</math> is a collection of local sections of <math>\mathcal{F}</math> satisfying a compatibility relation on every intersecting <math>A,B\in \mathcal{U}</math>

:<math>f(A)|_{A \cap B} = f(B)|_{A \cap B}</math>

A 1-cocycle <math>f</math> satisfies for every non-empty <math>U = A\cap B \cap C</math> with <math>A,B,C \in \mathcal{U}</math>

:<math>f(B \cap C)|_U - f(A \cap C)|_U + f(A \cap B)|_U = 0</math>

====Coboundary====
A ''q''-cochain is called a ''q''-coboundary if it is in the image of <math>\delta</math> and <math>B^q(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{F}) := \mathrm{Im} ( \delta_{q-1}) \subseteq C^{q}(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{F})</math> is the set of all ''q''-coboundaries.

For example, a 1-cochain <math>f</math> is a 1-coboundary if there exists a 0-cochain <math>h</math> such that for every intersecting <math>A,B\in \mathcal{U}</math>

:<math>f(A \cap B) = h(A)|_{A \cap B} - h(B)|_{A \cap B}</math>

===Cohomology===

The '''Čech cohomology''' of <math>\mathcal{U}</math> with values in <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is defined to be the cohomology of the cochain complex <math>(C^{\bullet}(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{F}), \delta)</math>. Thus the ''q''th Čech cohomology is given by

:<math>\check{H}^q(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{F}) := H^q((C^{\bullet}(\mathcal U, \mathcal F), \delta)) = Z^q(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{F}) / B^q(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{F})</math>.

The Čech cohomology of ''X'' is defined by considering [[Cover (topology)#Refinement|refinement]]s of open covers. If <math>\mathcal{V}</math> is a refinement of <math>\mathcal{U}</math> then there is a map in cohomology <math>\check{H}^*(\mathcal U,\mathcal F) \to \check{H}^*(\mathcal V,\mathcal F).</math> The open covers of ''X'' form a [[directed set]] under refinement, so the above map leads to a [[direct system (mathematics)|direct system]] of abelian groups. The '''Čech cohomology''' of ''X'' with values in ''<math>\mathcal{F}</math>'' is defined as the [[direct limit]] <math>\check{H}(X,\mathcal F) := \varinjlim_{\mathcal U} \check{H}(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)</math> of this system.

The Čech cohomology of ''X'' with coefficients in a fixed abelian group ''A'', denoted <math>\check{H}(X;A)</math>, is defined as <math>\check{H}(X,\mathcal{F}_A)</math> where <math>\mathcal{F}_A</math> is the [[constant sheaf]] on ''X'' determined by ''A''.

A variant of Čech cohomology, called '''numerable Čech cohomology''', is defined as above, except that all open covers considered are required to be ''numerable'': that is, there is a [[partition of unity]] {ρ<sub>''i''</sub>} such that each support <math>\{x\mid\rho_i(x)>0\}</math> is contained in some element of the cover. If ''X'' is [[paracompact]] and [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]], then numerable Čech cohomology agrees with the usual Čech cohomology.

==Relation to other cohomology theories==

If ''X'' is [[homotopy equivalent]] to a [[CW complex]], then the Čech cohomology <math>\check{H}^{*}(X;A)</math> is [[naturally isomorphic]] to the [[singular homology|singular cohomology]] <math> H^*(X;A) \,</math>. If ''X'' is a [[differentiable manifold]], then <math>\check{H}^*(X;\R)</math> is also naturally isomorphic to the [[de Rham cohomology]]; the article on de Rham cohomology provides a brief review of this isomorphism. For less well-behaved spaces, Čech cohomology differs from singular cohomology. For example if ''X'' is the [[topologist's sine curve|closed topologist's sine curve]], then <math>\check{H}^1(X;\Z)=\Z,</math> whereas <math>H^1(X;\Z)=0.</math>

If ''X'' is a differentiable manifold and the cover <math>\mathcal{U}</math> of ''X'' is a "good cover" (''i.e.'' all the sets ''U''<sub>α</sub> are [[Contractible space|contractible]] to a point, and all finite intersections of sets in <math>\mathcal{U}</math> are either empty or contractible to a point), then <math>\check{H}^{*}(\mathcal U;\R)</math> is isomorphic to the de Rham cohomology.

If ''X'' is compact Hausdorff, then Čech cohomology (with coefficients in a [[discrete group]]) is isomorphic to [[Alexander-Spanier cohomology]].

For a presheaf <math>\mathcal{F}</math> on ''X'', let <math>\mathcal{F}^+</math> denote its [[sheafification]]. Then we have a natural comparison map

:<math>\chi: \check{H}^*(X,\mathcal{F}) \to H^*(X,\mathcal{F}^+)</math>

from Čech cohomology to [[sheaf cohomology]]. If ''X'' is paracompact Hausdorff, then <math display="inline">\chi</math> is an isomorphism. More generally, <math display="inline">\chi</math> is an isomorphism whenever the Čech cohomology of all presheaves on ''X'' with zero sheafification vanishes.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Brady |first=Zarathustra |title=Notes on sheaf cohomology |url=https://math.mit.edu/~notzeb/sheaf-coh.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220617230348/https://math.mit.edu/~notzeb/sheaf-coh.pdf |archive-date=2022-06-17 |page=11}}</ref>

==In algebraic geometry==
Čech cohomology can be defined more generally for objects in a [[site (mathematics)|site]] '''C''' endowed with a topology. This applies, for example, to the Zariski site or the etale site of a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] ''X''. The Čech cohomology with values in some [[sheaf (mathematics)|sheaf]] <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is defined as

:<math>\check H^n (X, \mathcal{F}) := \varinjlim_{\mathcal U} \check H^n(\mathcal U, \mathcal{F}).</math>

where the [[colimit]] runs over all coverings (with respect to the chosen topology) of ''X''. Here <math>\check H^n(\mathcal U, \mathcal F)</math> is defined as above, except that the ''r''-fold intersections of open subsets inside the ambient topological space are replaced by the ''r''-fold [[fiber product]]

:<math>\mathcal U^{\times^r_X} := \mathcal U \times_X \dots \times_X \mathcal U.</math>

As in the classical situation of topological spaces, there is always a map

:<math>\check H^n(X, \mathcal F) \rightarrow H^n(X, \mathcal F)</math>

from Čech cohomology to sheaf cohomology. It is always an isomorphism in degrees ''n'' = 0 and 1, but may fail to be so in general. For the [[Zariski topology]] on a [[Noetherian topological space|Noetherian]] [[separated scheme]], Čech and sheaf cohomology agree for any [[quasi-coherent sheaf]]. For the [[étale topology]], the two cohomologies agree for any étale sheaf on ''X'', provided that any [[finite set]] of points of ''X'' are contained in some open affine subscheme. This is satisfied, for example, if ''X'' is [[quasi-projective variety|quasi-projective]] over an [[affine scheme]].<ref>{{Citation | last1=Milne | first1=James S. | title=Étale cohomology | url=https://books.google.com/books?isbn=978-0-691-08238-7 | publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] | series=Princeton Mathematical Series | isbn=978-0-691-08238-7 |mr=559531 | year=1980 | volume=33 |chapter=Section III.2, Theorem 2.17}}</ref>

The possible difference between Čech cohomology and sheaf cohomology is a motivation for the use of [[hypercovering]]s: these are more general objects than the Čech [[nerve (category theory)|nerve]]

:<math>N_X \mathcal U : \dots \to \mathcal U \times_X \mathcal U \times_X \mathcal U \to \mathcal U \times_X \mathcal U \to \mathcal U.</math>

A hypercovering ''K''<sub>∗</sub> of ''X'' is a certain [[simplicial object]] in '''C''', i.e., a collection of objects ''K''<sub>''n''</sub> together with boundary and degeneracy maps. Applying a sheaf <math>\mathcal{F}</math> to ''K''<sub>∗</sub> yields a [[simplicial abelian group]] <math display="inline">\mathcal{F}(K_\ast)</math> whose ''n''-th cohomology group is denoted <math display="inline">H^n(\mathcal F (K_\ast))</math>. (This group is the same as <math>\check H^n(\mathcal U, \mathcal F)</math> in case ''K''<sub>∗</sub> equals <math>N_X \mathcal U </math>.) Then, it can be shown that there is a canonical isomorphism

:<math>H^n (X, \mathcal F) \cong \varinjlim_{K_*} H^n(\mathcal F(K_*)),</math>

where the colimit now runs over all hypercoverings.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Artin | first1=Michael | author1-link=Michael Artin | last2=Mazur | first2=Barry | author2-link=Barry Mazur | title=Etale homotopy | publisher=Springer | series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics |volume=100 | year=1969 |chapter=Theorem 8.16 |chapter-url={{GBurl|2pR8CwAAQBAJ|p=98}} |page=98 |isbn=978-3-540-36142-8}}</ref>

=== Examples ===
The most basic example of Čech cohomology is given by the case where the presheaf <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is a [[constant sheaf]], e.g. <math>\mathcal{F}=\mathbb{R}</math>. In such cases, each <math>q</math>-cochain <math>f</math> is simply a function which maps every <math>q</math>-simplex to <math>\mathbb{R}</math>. For example, we calculate the first Čech cohomology with values in <math>\mathbb{R}</math> of the unit circle <math>X=S^1</math>. Dividing <math>X</math> into three arcs and choosing sufficiently small open neighborhoods, we obtain an open cover <math>\mathcal{U}=\{U_0,U_1,U_2\}</math> where <math>U_i \cap U_j \ne \emptyset</math> but <math>U_0 \cap U_1 \cap U_2 = \emptyset</math>.

Given any 1-cocycle <math>f</math>, <math>\delta f</math> is a 2-cochain which takes inputs of the form <math>(U_i,U_i,U_i),(U_i,U_i,U_j),(U_j,U_i,U_i),(U_i,U_j,U_i)</math> where <math>i \ne j</math> (since <math>U_0 \cap U_1 \cap U_2 = \emptyset</math> and hence <math>(U_i,U_j,U_k)</math> is not a 2-simplex for any permutation <math>\{i,j,k\}=\{1,2,3\}</math>). The first three inputs give <math>f(U_i,U_i)=0</math>; the fourth gives

:<math>\delta f(U_i,U_j,U_i)=f(U_j,U_i)-f(U_i,U_i)+f(U_i,U_j)=0 \implies f(U_j,U_i)=-f(U_i,U_j).</math>

Such a function is fully determined by the values of <math>f(U_0,U_1),f(U_0,U_2),f(U_1,U_2)</math>. Thus,

:<math>Z^1(\mathcal{U},\mathbb{R})=\{f \in C^1(\mathcal{U},\mathbb{R}) : f(U_i,U_i)=0, f(U_j,U_i)=-f(U_i,U_j)\} \cong \mathbb{R}^3.</math>

On the other hand, given any 1-coboundary <math>f = \delta g</math>, we have

:<math>\begin{cases}
f(U_i,U_i)=g(U_i)-g(U_i)=0 & (i=0,1,2); \\
f(U_i,U_j)=g(U_j)-g(U_i)=-f(U_j,U_i) & (i \ne j)
\end{cases}</math>

However, upon closer inspection we see that <math>f(U_0,U_1)+f(U_1,U_2)=f(U_0,U_2)</math> and hence each 1-coboundary <math>f</math> is uniquely determined by <math>f(U_0,U_1)</math> and <math>f(U_1,U_2)</math>. This gives the set of 1-coboundaries:

:<math>\begin{align}
B^1(\mathcal{U},\mathbb{R})=\{f \in C^1(\mathcal{U},\mathbb{R}) : \ & f(U_i,U_i)=0, f(U_j,U_i)=-f(U_i,U_j), \\
&f(U_0,U_2)=f(U_0,U_1)+f(U_1,U_2)\} \cong \mathbb{R}^2.
\end{align}</math>

Therefore, <math>\check{H}^1(\mathcal{U},\mathbb{R})=Z^1(\mathcal{U},\mathbb{R})/B^1(\mathcal{U},\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}</math>. Since <math>\mathcal{U}</math> is a [[good cover]] of <math>X</math>, we have <math>\check{H}^1(X,\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}</math> by [[Leray's theorem]].

We may also compute the [[coherent sheaf cohomology]] of <math>\Omega^1</math> on the projective line <math>\mathbb{P}^1_\mathbb{C}</math> using the Čech complex. Using the cover

:<math>\mathcal{U} = \{ U_1 = \text{Spec}(\Complex[y]), U_2 = \text{Spec}(\Complex[y^{-1}]) \}</math>

we have the following modules from the cotangent sheaf

:<math>\begin{align}
&\Omega^1(U_1) = \Complex[y]dy \\
&\Omega^1(U_2) = \Complex \left [y^{-1} \right ]dy^{-1}
\end{align}</math>

If we take the conventions that <math>dy^{-1} = -(1/y^2)dy</math> then we get the Čech complex

:<math>0 \to \Complex[y]dy \oplus \Complex \left [y^{-1} \right ]dy^{-1} \xrightarrow{d^0} \Complex \left [y,y^{-1} \right ]dy \to 0</math>

Since <math>d^0</math> is injective and the only element not in the image of <math>d^0</math> is <math>y^{-1}dy</math> we get that

:<math>\begin{align}
&H^1(\mathbb{P}_{\Complex}^1,\Omega^1) \cong \Complex \\
&H^k(\mathbb{P}_{\Complex}^1,\Omega^1) \cong 0 \text{ for } k \neq 1
\end{align}</math>
